title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM-Generated Network Configuration Changes
abstract: We report a preregistered paired experiment that tested whether deterministic tool-augmentation (generate → deterministic verifier/sandbox → optional repair) changes the rate of unsafe network-change proposals produced by a hosted LLM on intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 synthetic, preregistered tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM-only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt-5-mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Crucial preregistered detail: per-pair generation used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM candidate shared across arms). Observed (confirmatory, adversarial-cluster): baseline unsafe proposals = 0/200; guarded unsafe proposals = 0/200 (paired contingency n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). Paired risk difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_resamples=10000; seed=1729). Statistical clarification: with zero discordant pairs the McNemar test is non-informative for detecting a verifier causal effect here—the paired design and shared-generation semantics produced identical initial candidates and therefore prevented observing verifier-mediated corrections when the shared candidate was already valid. We archive execution and analysis artifacts (see execution manifest) and discuss how shared-generation semantics, task-bank ceiling effects, adversarial-strength coverage, and single-model scope explain the null outcome. We recommend alternative preregistered designs (independent per-arm generation, stronger adversarial templates, multiple models, and verifier stress tests) for future confirmatory tests.

sections.introduction: Automating intent-driven network configuration with large language models promises operator efficiency but raises operational-safety risks: erroneous changes can violate reachability, break services, or cause outages. Prior proposals remedy risk by augmenting LLMs with deterministic validators, sandbox simulators, and guarded execution gates. We evaluated whether a deterministic verifier pipeline reduces the rate of verifier-detected unsafe configuration proposals in a preregistered, paired experiment. Research question (final, preregistered): How does deterministic tool-augmentation (generate → deterministic verifier/sandbox → automatic refinement) change the rate of unsafe network-change proposals produced by a hosted LLM under benign and adversarial NetOps prompts? Principal contributions: (1) a machine-readable preregistered paired confirmatory experiment comparing baseline LLM-only vs a guarded pipeline on N=200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks; (2) a full, archived execution and deterministic analysis showing both arms produced zero verifier-detected unsafe proposals under the preregistered conditions; (3) a focused statistical and methodological diagnosis explaining why the preregistered shared-generation semantics and task-bank design produced a ceiling effect that made the confirmatory paired test non-informative, plus concrete recommendations for repeat confirmatory designs.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and prototypes document rapid uptake of LLMs for NetOps tasks (intent translation, configuration generation, AIOps co-pilots) and argue for tool grounding and verification-in-the-loop to improve operational trust (representative records: Bilal et al. (arXiv:2605.12729), Ferrag et al., 6G-Bench (IEEE OJCOMS 2026)). Independent work across high-stakes domains shows that tool-augmentation and generate–verify–refine pipelines can increase measured correctness, but gains depend on task bank, verifier fidelity, and adversarial coverage. Method papers recommend workflow-centred, sandboxed evaluations and governance layers (MCP/schemas, approval gates) to measure agentic NetOps reliability. Our experiment was designed to contribute reproducible, preregistered evidence about a deterministic verifier’s effect under controlled paired conditions, addressing a gap in adversarial, workflow-centred NetOps evaluations.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered before execution (machine-readable plan defining sampling, estimands, analysis, exclusions, and stopping rules). Confirmatory estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (paired difference in unsafe-proposal rate: guarded minus baseline) analyzed with an exact McNemar two-sided test; primary alpha=0.05. Sampling: deterministic task generator produced 200 unique synthetic tasks (single-AS multi-device topologies, intents targeting IPv4 reachability, ACL/policy and ordered workflow constraints). Paired contract and generation semantics: to control model-call budget and generation noise the preregistration used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation=false): for each task a single initial candidate was generated and shared between arms; the guarded arm then handed that candidate to the deterministic validator. Model and orchestration: declared model = gpt-5-mini served via the recorded adapter openai_responses; orchestration used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. Validator and analysis: guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (sandbox intent-constraint validator); analysis executor = paired_binary_analysis_v1. Power assumptions: preregistered power calculations targeted a detectable paired reduction ≈7 percentage points assuming a nontrivial baseline unsafe rate (~10–15%). Pre-specified exclusion/retry rules, sensitivity analyses (treating technical failures as safe/unsafe), and exploratory diagnostics (refusal rate, verifier ROC) were recorded in the preregistration. Execution and archives: planned 400 episodes (200 tasks × 2 arms). Because of shared-generation semantics the run used model_calls_used=200 (one generation per task) and completed all episodes; execution and scoring artifacts are archived in the execution manifest and analysis artifacts (see archived bundle).
sections.results: Execution accounting: completed paired episodes = 200 pairs (400 episodes completed), model_calls_used = 200 (shared initial candidate per pair), failed episodes = 0. Confirmatory outcome (adversarial cluster, preregistered): definition—success = no verifier-detected violation (binary outcome = 0 for unsafe proposal, 1 for safe). Observed counts: baseline successes = 200/200; guarded successes = 200/200. Paired contingency: n11 = 200 (both arms safe), n10 = 0 (guarded safe, baseline unsafe), n01 = 0 (guarded unsafe, baseline safe), n00 = 0 (both unsafe). Paired estimand: risk difference (guarded minus baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided p-value = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, resamples=10000, seed=1729) on difference = [0.0, 0.0]. Exploratory diagnostics: preregistered refusal-rate and verifier-ROC diagnostics were not produced because there were no verifier refusals or discordant cases in this run. Representative scoring and validator traces for example tasks (e.g., pair-000001) and the full analysis artifacts (condition_summary.csv, paired_contingency_table.csv, paired_difference_figure.svg) are archived in the execution bundle (see execution_manifest and analysis_artifacts).
sections.discussion: Statistical and causal interpretation: the observed contingency (n10=n01=0) implies zero discordant pairs. McNemar-style paired tests detect within-pair changes; with zero discordant pairs the test is non-informative about a causal verifier effect under the sampled conditions—an outcome arising from the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics combined with a task bank that produced valid initial candidates for this model. Importantly, the null numeric result (difference=0.0, p=1.0) must not be interpreted as general evidence that guarded pipelines are ineffective. Instead, it documents that under these specific preregistered conditions (shared-generation, the selected synthetic tasks, the single declared model, and the deterministic validator) there was no opportunity for the verifier to change outcomes because the initial candidates were already valid. Causes and lessons: (1) shared_initial_candidate semantics constrain the experiment’s ability to observe verifier-mediated corrections—independent per-arm generation is required when the hypothesis concerns the verifier’s causal ability to reject or repair invalid candidates; (2) ceiling effects in synthetic task banks (tasks that are too easy relative to the model) remove statistical power and invalidate preregistered power assumptions (the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0% rather than the preregistered ≈10–15%); (3) adversarial-cluster strength matters—the adversarial templates used here did not elicit unsafe outputs from the declared model on the sampled tasks; (4) single-model scope limits external validity. Operational implication: evaluators that aim to measure verifier impact should (a) avoid ceilinged tasks, (b) use independent per-condition generation when evaluating verifier causal effects, (c) include systematically stronger adversarial templates and model diversity, and (d) record verifier operating characteristics (false-negative/false-positive trade-offs) in exploratory runs. Recommendations for a repeat confirmatory test (preregister in advance): independent per-arm generation, an increased number of adversarially strengthened tasks sampled to produce a nonzero baseline unsafe rate, multiple LLMs, and explicit verifier stress tests that include obfuscation patterns known to elicit validator false negatives.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment comparing an LLM-only baseline to a deterministic verifier-augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Observed verifier-detected unsafe proposals were zero in both arms (paired difference 0.0; p=1.0). A methodological diagnosis shows this null result is due to preregistered shared-generation semantics and a ceilinged task bank that produced no discordant pairs; consequently the paired test was non-informative for the preregistered causal question. The study illustrates how preregistered generation semantics and task-bank design determine whether verifier benefits can be empirically detected. We release archived execution and analysis artifacts (execution_manifest and analysis_artifacts) to enable reproducible follow-ups that adopt independent per-arm generation, stronger adversarial tasks, and multi-model coverage to properly test verifier effectiveness.

limitations: Synthetic-task domain and coverage: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies limited to single-AS multi-device setups (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5); results may not generalize to production, multi-AS, or vendor-specific features.

Shared-generation semantics: the preregistered design used shared_initial_candidate per paired task (independent_condition_generation=false). This produced identical initial candidates for baseline and guarded arms, creating a ceiling effect when those candidates were valid and preventing observation of verifier-driven differences in those cases.

Adversarial prompt strength: although an adversarial cluster was preregistered, the adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt-5-mini on the sampled tasks; more diverse and stronger adversarial cases are needed.
Single-model scope: only the declared model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; no claims of multi-model generality are supported.

Verifier validation scope: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 operated deterministically on archived synthetic sandboxed states; external independent validation of validator completeness against all real-world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator-in-the-loop workload measurement, nor multi-vendor interoperability field trials were performed; operator-cost trade-offs (false refusals, extra verification workload) remain unquantified at scale.
